html:
Macedon was an ancient kingdom in northern Greece that, under Philip II and his son Alexander, rose from a border state to the conqueror of Greece and the Persian Empire. The chart's bar starts with Philip's accession in 359 BCE and ends with the Roman victory at Pydna in 168 BCE.

The kingdom was much older, ruled by the Argead dynasty, but southern Greeks saw it as half barbarian. Philip changed that. He built a professional army around the phalanx of pikemen with a strong cavalry, took gold mines in Thrace, and beat Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE. Greek cities were then joined in a league under his lead.

Philip was murdered in 336 BCE. Alexander used his father's army to destroy the Achaemenid Empire and march as far as India in eleven years of conquest. His teacher had been Aristotle.

After Alexander died in 323 BCE, his generals split the empire. The Seleucids took Asia, the Ptolemies took Egypt, and Macedon itself, after years of fighting, went to the Antigonid dynasty. It stayed a strong power in Greece until it ran into the Roman Republic. Rome won three wars against it, abolished the monarchy after Pydna, and made Macedonia a Roman province in 146 BCE.
